paper_title: Foundation4D: Towards a unified perception and reconstruction model for autonomous vehicles

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: We introduce Foundation4D, a unified feed-forward model for geometry estimation, 3D detection, semantic occupancy, and Gaussian reconstruction from multi-camera driving video. A shared backbone uses factorized spatiotemporal attention to efficiently combine observations across cameras and time. Our video inference pipeline uses pose graph optimization to refine camera trajectories and assembles object tracks across input windows. We also develop a data annotation pipeline and release PAI-Foundation4D, a benchmark with dense depth and semantic occupancy labels for 1,253 driving clips. With benchmark-specific fine-tuning, Foundation4D achieves the lowest depth AbsRel on Waymo and nuScenes, the highest detection mAP on nuScenes, and the highest occupancy mIoU on OpenOccupancy among the compared methods. Our task-combination study shows benefits for both detection and geometry: co-training detection with geometry and occupancy improves top-class mAP by 1.2 points over detection-only training, while co-training geometry with detection reduces camera-to-rig translation error by $13.4\%$ relative to geometry-only training. We further use the predicted geometry and trajectories as priors for lidarless NuRec, supporting reconstruction of driving scenes for simulation.

and reconstruction model for autonomous vehicles 1. Introduction Two central goals in the development of autonomous vehicle systems are understanding the driving environment and reconstructing recorded scenes for simulation. Both require recovering scene geometry, objects, their motion, and the space they occupy. Unified perception models learn these capabilities through shared visual representations, avoiding the repeated processing of the same observations by separate networks. UniAD and PARA-Drive connect perception with prediction and planning [1, 2], while GeoUP jointly predicts depth, 3D objects, and semantic occupancy from driving video [3]. These outputs capture much of the structure and motion needed for scene reconstruction. Simulation additionally requires recovering scene appearance so that the environment and its moving actors can be rendered from novel viewpoints. Unifying perception and reconstruction would therefore enable shared model to both understand real driving scenes and recreate them for simulation. Recent progress in feed-forward reconstruction offers basis for this integration. VGGT [4] jointly recovers camera parameters and dense geometry from multiple images, while Gaussian reconstruction models such as Instant NuRec [5] predict renderable driving scenes without per-scene optimization. These advances make it possible to infer scene structure and appearance directly from images, but extending them to shared model for multi-camera video requires efficient use of observations across views and time. In particular, the global attention used in VGGT grows quadratically with the total number of image tokens, making longer sequences costly to process. We present Foundation4D, feed-forward model for driving perception and reconstruction. shared backbone extracts features from multi-camera video, and task-specific decoders predict camera poses and metric depth, 3D objects, semantic occupancy, and Gaussian attributes in single pass over an input window. Factorized spatiotemporal attention reduces the cost of combining information across cameras and time. To use these predictions over complete driving recording, geometric estimates must remain aligned and object identities must be maintained across windows. Our video-level inference pipeline assembles the window predictions into scene geometry and camera and object trajectories over long sequences. These outputs support Gaussian scene reconstruction and also provide priors for lidarless NuRec [6], demonstrating their use in downstream neural reconstruction workflow. Training and evaluating these capabilities requires dense annotations that remain aligned with the changing scene. Sparse LiDAR observations can be combined to improve surface coverage, but vehicle and object motion make it difficult to align these measurements with camera images. Asynchronous sensing and rolling-shutter exposure further complicate this alignment. We provide pipeline for the creation of accurate depth images and semantic occupancy. We release the PAIFoundation4D benchmark [7], 1,253 clips of the Physical AI Autonomous Vehicles (PAI) dataset [8] that support geometry, detection, and occupancy evaluation on the same driving scenes. By providing dense annotations together with documented evaluation protocols, the benchmark gives the community common basis for comparing methods and measuring progress across these tasks. We evaluate Foundation4D on established public benchmarks and PAIFoundation4D. With benchmarkspecific fine-tuning, it achieves the lowest depth error on Waymo [9] and nuScenes [10], the highest detection accuracy on nuScenes, and the highest semantic occupancy accuracy on OpenOccupancy [11] among the compared methods. Our evaluations show that Foundation4D can be adapted effectively across driving datasets. Longer temporal context improves detection without retraining, while pose graph optimization (PGO) with motion prior improves camera trajectory accuracy over sequential stitching on PAI (Tabs. 4 and 9). Our task-combination study also reveals benefits and trade-offs of joint perception learning, with gains that depend on the tasks being combined. Our reconstruction experiments show that using predicted ego poses preserves overall rendering quality close to that obtained with ground-truth ego poses (Tab. 15). The predicted geometry and actor trajectories 3 Foundation4D: Towards unified perception and reconstruction model for autonomous vehicles also provide useful priors for lidarless NuRec [6], demonstrating their practical value in reconstructing driving scenes for simulation. Our contributions are: Foundation4D, feed-forward perception and reconstruction model that shares multi-camera video features across task-specific decoders for geometry, semantics, objects, occupancy, and Gaussian reconstruction. video-level inference pipeline that aligns window-level geometry and assembles object trajectories, improving trajectory estimation over long driving sequences. data annotation pipeline that accounts for sensor timing, ego and actor motion, and visibility to generate depth and semantic occupancy labels from driving recordings. The PAIFoundation4D benchmark, with dense annotations and evaluation protocols for comparing geometry, detection, and occupancy methods on common set of driving scenes. 2. Related work Foundation4D brings geometric recovery, semantic perception, and Gaussian reconstruction into shared model for multi-camera driving video. It builds on two closely related research directions: multi-task learning for autonomous driving, perception and reconstruction tasks. 2.1. Multi-task learning for autonomous driving Multi-task learning allows driving models to share features across different descriptions of the same scene. PnPNet [12] and ViP3D [13] jointly model detection, tracking, and motion forecasting, while BEVFormer [14] and PETRv2 [15] explore shared representations for detection and segmentation. UniVision [16] jointly learns 3D detection and occupancy through interacting BEV and voxel features. Planning-oriented approaches further connect scene understanding to driving decisions [17, 18, 19]. UniAD [1] passes information between perception, prediction, and planning through task queries; PARA-Drive [2] studies these dependencies and co-trains parallel task heads through shared BEV features. The benefits of joint learning depend on which tasks are combined [20], making task interactions an important consideration alongside the range of outputs model supports. Pretraining offers complementary route to representations that support multiple tasks. UniPAD [21] learns transferable features through volumetric rendering with image and depth reconstruction objectives, while DriveWorld [22] uses temporal scene and action prediction for downstream adaptation. Geometric foundation models such as VGGT [4] learn multi-image features for recovering cameras and dense scene structure. These reconstruction objectives provide geometric basis for extending shared backbone to driving perception. Recent driving models extend geometric representations to perception and planning. DVGT-2 [23] couples streaming geometry reconstruction with trajectory planning. Closely related to our approach, GeoUP [3] adapts VGGT to calibrated multi-camera video through factorized temporal and cross-view attention, conditioning its features on known camera intrinsics and poses. It jointly predicts metric depth, 3D objects, and semantic occupancy, with auxiliary camera-pose supervision and multi-dataset training that accommodates missing task annotations. USR-Drive [24] connects object detection and renderable reconstruction by jointly denoising 3D box and Gaussian latents from multi-view video with known camera poses. Foundation4D combines geometric and semantic perception with Gaussian reconstruction in shared feed-forward model, while explicitly estimating ego motion and camera-to-rig calibration. We train the shared model on large-scale, partially annotated driving data and examine transfer and interference between geometry, detection, and occupancy. 4 Foundation4D: Towards unified perception and reconstruction model for autonomous vehicles 2.2. Perception and reconstruction tasks Geometric reconstruction. Feed-forward geometry models learn to recover 3D structure and camera geometry from images. DUSt3R and MASt3R establish pointmapand correspondence-based reconstruction [25, 26], while VGGT [4] jointly predicts cameras and dense geometry from multiple images. Related models explore alternative geometric parameterizations [27, 28], optional camera and depth priors [29, 30], and efficient multi-image inference [31, 32, 33]. Temporal extensions maintain scene state or cached features for incremental reconstruction [34, 35, 36], while dynamic models recover time-varying structure and point trajectories [37, 38, 39]. Driving adaptations exploit the fixed relationships between vehicle-mounted cameras and the motion of the rig. DVGT [40] predicts metric pointmaps and ego poses from multi-camera images without supplied calibration. Rig3R [41] supports optional rig metadata and inference of missing camera geometry. With calibration available, DriveVGGT [42] uses calibration-guided attention and factorized heads for rig geometry and ego motion. TRIG [43] instead separates trajectory and rig priors in feature encoding and supervision while retaining the VGGT prediction heads. LiAuto-GeoX [44] addresses inference efficiency by distilling dense geometry and cross-view relations into compact student. Scaling reconstruction to long videos requires managing memory and accumulated drift. DVGT-2 [23] carries temporal information through sliding-window cache, while Drive3R [45] combines block-wise causal attention with confidence-aware re-anchoring under known camera calibration. Complementary systems assemble local reconstructions through geometric alignment and global optimization. VGGT-Long [46] aligns overlapping chunks with confidence-weighted similarity transforms and uses loop constraints to correct drift. VGGTSLAM [47] optimizes submap alignments on SL(4) to account for projective ambiguity. VGGT-SLAM 2.0 [48] refines keyframe-level geometry through constraints within and between submaps, and uses VGGT attention to verify loop closures. Foundation4D adapts this local-to-global strategy to driving video, where multiple cameras move as one rig but may capture images at different times. We separate camera-to-rig calibration from ego motion so that overlapping windows can constrain shared trajectory, whose corrections are propagated to each camera at its own capture time (Sec. 5). 3D Object detection and tracking. Camera-based 3D object detection localizes and classifies surrounding objects as oriented 3D cuboids from multi-camera images, while multi-object tracking links these detections into identity-consistent trajectories over time. Query-based detectors build on the set prediction of DETR [49], decoding sparse set of object queries that are matched one-to-one to the ground truth without anchors or non-maximum suppression. They differ mainly in how queries gather multi-view image features. Dense-attention methods make image features 3Daware for global cross-attention. PETR [50] adds position embeddings computed from camera frustums, while 3DPPE [51] replaces them with 3D point embeddings derived from predicted depth. Sparse methods instead sample features around 3D anchors or BEV pillar queries across views and frames [52, 53]. Temporal fusion further improves localization and velocity estimation. PETRv2 [15] aligns past-frame coordinates with ego motion, StreamPETR [54] propagates object queries through memory queue for efficient streaming detection, Stream3DPPE [51] and RoPETR [55] extend StreamPETR with point embeddings and spatio-temporal rotary position embeddings, respectively. RayDN [56] improves training by extending query denoising [57] with hard negatives sampled along camera rays, which suppresses duplicate detections at wrong depths. These detectors aggregate views and frames inside the detection head, using ego poses to align past frames. GeoUP [3] instead fuses them in VGGT-initialized backbone conditioned on camera calibration and ego poses (Sec. 2.1) and decodes boxes with RayDN-style head, reporting state-of-the-art nuScenes results. Foundation4D likewise aggregates images from all cameras across temporal window in its geometry-pretrained backbone and decodes PETR-style queries into 3D boxes and velocities through deformable attention [58]. Unlike GeoUP, which 5 Foundation4D: Towards unified perception and reconstruction model for autonomous vehicles requires ground-truth ego poses, Foundation4D predicts them directly from multi-view images. Tracking methods aim to obtain temporally consistent object trajectories and differ in how they associate detections over time. Following the tracking by detection paradigm, SORT [59] combines Kalman-filter motion prediction with Hungarian matching, AB3DMOT [60] extends this design to 3D boxes, and CenterPoint [61] matches detections using their predicted velocities. Query-based trackers such as TrackFormer [62] and MOTR [63] instead propagate track queries from frame to frame, an approach that MUTR3D [64] and PFTrack [65] bring to multi-camera 3D tracking. These online trackers rely on past observations, whereas offline methods optimize association over many frames at once. MPNTrack [66] learns it with message passing on detection graph. SUSHI [67] scales learned association to long clips through hierarchy of graphs over increasingly long time spans. Foundation4D takes inspiration from the offline literature, but adopts simple yet effective association mechanism from online methods. It utilizes Kalman-filter consuming velocities predicted by our detection head, and uses and Hungarian association for frame-by frame association, similar to SORT and AB3DMOT. However, it processes the clip offline, reconnecting fragmented tracks in second pass and refining each trajectory with RauchTungStriebel (RTS) smoother that also uses later observations. Semantic occupancy. Semantic occupancy prediction tackles scene geometry beyond visible surfaces, completing the surrounding geometry and assigning semantic labels to occupied regions. Existing approaches can be grouped according to their latent scene representations into plane-based, dense volumetric, and sparse methods, with hybrid methods connecting these families. Plane-based approaches encode scenes using two-dimensional feature grids. BEVFormer [14] learns BEV features through spatiotemporal attention, while TPVFormer [68] uses three orthogonal feature planes. SelfOcc [69] investigates BEV and TPV representations under self-supervised training, and POP-3D [70] uses TPV features for open-vocabulary occupancy prediction. Dense volumetric approaches maintain features on regular 3D voxel grids. MonoScene [71] and SurroundOcc [72] use 3D convolutions, OccFormer [73] uses dual-path transformer, and OccMamba [74] applies state space models. OccGen [75] uses diffusion-based refinement, PanoOcc [76] aggregates multi-view and temporal features through voxel queries, and COTR [77] learns compact geometry-aware volumetric features. Allocating features to empty regions introduces memory and computational costs, motivating sparse alternatives. SparseOcc [78] operates on sparse voxel tensors. OPUS [79] predicts occupied locations and semantic classes directly from learned queries, SPSC [80] progressively prunes unoccupied queries during coarse-to-fine refinement, and GaussianFormer [81] represents scenes with sparse semantic Gaussian primitives. Hybrid designs combine these representation choices. VoxFormer [82] expands depth-guided sparse voxel queries into dense volume, while CONet [11] refines coarse occupied voxels at higher resolution. Symphonies [83] connects contextual instance queries with image and voxel features, and CGFormer [84] combines voxel and tri-perspective features. Foundation4D adopts BEV representation for semantic occupancy at 20 cm resolution and up to 100 ahead of the ego vehicle. This compact BEV representation limits memory use, allowing us to support semantic occupancy alongside the other output tasks within unified multi-camera, multi-timestamp model. Gaussian scene reconstruction. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [85] represents scene with explicit anisotropic primitives for novel-view rendering. Feed-forward methods learn to predict these primitives across scenes, reducing the need to optimize each new scene separately. Representative approaches include pixelSplat [86] and MVSplat [87] for sparseview reconstruction, and GS-LRM [88] for transformer-based Gaussian prediction. DepthSplat [89] connects multi-view depth estimation with Gaussian reconstruction, while NoPoSplat [90] predicts Gaussians from unposed images. Geometry foundation models provide further route to feed-forward rendering: AnySplat [91] extends VGGT-based geometry transformer with Gaussian prediction and distills camera and geometry priors from pretrained VGGT. DrivingGaussian [93], Street Gaussians [94], and OmniRe [95] reconstruct static backgrounds and dynamic actors through per-sequence optimization. Feed-forward approaches such as STORM [96] and DrivingForward [97] address sparse temporal observations and surround-view inputs, while DGGT [98] jointly estimates cameras, Gaussians, and scene motion. Physical AI Autonomous Vehicles Foundation4D Physical AI Autonomous Vehicles (PAI) [8] provides multi-sensor driving recordings for autonomous vehicle research, including multi-camera RGB videos, LiDAR point clouds, and radar detections. The dataset also provides sensor calibration, ego-motion trajectories, and automatically generated 3D cuboid tracks with object poses, dimensions, semantic classes, and track identifiers. We augment the PAI sequences used in our benchmark with LiDAR-derived depth maps and occupancy grids with per-voxel semantic and velocity labels for dense 3D perception evaluation [7]. Our geometry, detection, and semantic occupancy evaluations use the same 1,253 PAI test clips and six cameras. Task-specific protocols are described in Sec. 7. The annotation pipeline aggregates static LiDAR points across time and combines motion-compensated dynamic points within local temporal windows. As auxiliary inputs, it uses semantic masks precomputed by an internal semantic segmentation model and instance masks generated by SAM 2 [108] using box prompts derived from projected 3D cuboids. Camera calibration and sensor poses align LiDAR points across time and camera views, while cuboid tracks guide motion compensation and supplement image semantic predictions with cuboid class labels. The pipeline generates two outputs: depth maps rendered in each camera view and semantic occupancy grids in the vehicle frame. Fig. 4 summarizes the annotation pipeline, and Fig. 5 illustrates the resulting depth and semantic occupancy annotations on two PAI examples. 6.1. Temporal LiDAR aggregation Single LiDAR scans sparsely sample the scene, so we accumulate measurements over time to obtain more complete surface coverage. We compensate each return for ego motion using its acquisition timestamp and transform it into common world frame. Cuboid tracks identify actors that require motion compensation: static points are accumulated across the full clip, while dynamic points are collected from local window of up to ten LiDAR scans and warped to the actor pose at the target timestamp. This separation increases coverage while preserving the positions of moving objects. Smoothed cuboid trajectories are used to classify tracks as static or dynamic. For dynamic tracks, we interpolate the original cuboid poses to select points within padded cuboid crops and align them across time. Ground points within these crops are excluded from object reconstruction, with only high-confidence ground returns restored to the static cloud. The accumulated static cloud is then filtered by local density while preserving sparse planar surfaces supported by multiple scans. The pipeline also supports optional intensity filtering, with separate thresholds for static and dynamic returns. 17 Foundation4D: Towards unified perception and reconstruction model for autonomous vehicles Figure 4: PAI depth and occupancy annotation pipeline. The pipeline combines temporally aggregated LiDAR, cuboid tracks, and image masks to generate camera-view depth maps and vehicle-frame occupancy grids with per-voxel semantic and velocity labels. The shared legend indicates depth in meters and semantic classes. Foundation4D: Towards unified perception and reconstruction model for autonomous vehicles 6.2. Depth annotation generation We generate metric depth maps by rendering the accumulated static scene and motion-compensated actors into each camera view. Projection uses calibrated intrinsics and extrinsics at the cameras native resolution, accounting for camera motion during rolling-shutter exposure. Static depth is obtained from the nearest visible projected LiDAR point; dynamic points are rendered with fixed-radius Gaussian splats. Dynamic depth is integrated into the static depth map where instance masks overlap with dynamic semantic regions, subject to occlusion checks. Objects without instance masks use direct point projection. Visibility checks prevent occluded points from contributing to the depth map. We compare candidate depths against measured static depth and an auxiliary splatted reference, rendered from the static cloud, using the latter only where it is consistent with nearby measurements and semantic labels. Within masked dynamic regions, pixels without rendered dynamic depth are marked invalid instead of retaining background depth. Static depth is retained when dynamic prediction is rejected by occlusion checks. Visible dynamic points from direct projection can fill missing depth. Each valid output stores distance along the camera viewing ray in meters. Missing depth, sky, and ego-vehicle pixels are set to zero. 6.3. Semantic occupancy annotation generation We construct semantic occupancy annotations by assigning classes to the accumulated 3D points and voxelizing them in the target vehicle frame. Static points receive depth-consistent semantic votes from precomputed image semantic segmentation maps across multiple cameras and frames, with greater weight given to nearer observations. These votes are supplemented by the classes of static cuboid tracks. The highest accumulated weighted score determines each static points label, while dynamic points inherit the class of their associated cuboid track. Traffic-sign and traffic-light labels are then refined by propagating them from dense labeled regions to nearby connected points in 3D. Unlabeled and sky points are removed before constructing the static occupancy map. The static cloud is pre-voxelized in the world frame and cleaned to remove isolated components. At the end timestamp of each front wide-angle camera frame, we transform the static voxel centers and motioncompensated dynamic points into the vehicle frame. The exported grid uses 0.1 cubic voxels over 𝑥 [150, 150) m, 𝑦 [100, 100) m, and 𝑧 [3, 5) m. Static voxel centers and dynamic points are voxelized separately, with majority voting within each set. Dynamic voxels take precedence where the two sets overlap, except where static voxels represent road, sidewalk, or terrain. Each occupied voxel also stores 3D velocity in meters per second, representing world-relative motion expressed in vehicle coordinates. Here, static voxels have zero velocity while dynamic voxels inherit their tracks translational velocity, estimated from successive cuboid centers. 7. Application to lidarless NuRec We apply Foundation4D to lidarless NuRec [6], using its camera trajectories, dense geometry, and actor tracks as priors for scene reconstruction. This application complements the feed-forward Gaussian decoder in Sec. 3.7: NuRec optimizes separate Gaussian representation for each scene against the recorded images. 8.1. Reconstruction workflow The workflow in Fig. 18 takes multi-camera video and vehicle GPS/IMU trajectories as recorded inputs. Videolevel processing assembles poses and depth predicted from images by Foundation4D into camera trajectories and fused point cloud, which initializes reconstruction geometry. Detection and tracking provide oriented cuboids with persistent actor identities, separating moving objects from the static scene and associating their observations over time. These outputs replace priors previously obtained from LiDAR or separate reconstruction and perception pipelines. NuRec uses them to optimize dynamic Gaussian scene against RGB observations for novel-view rendering [85, 99]. 8.2. Limitations and open questions Unified model. Adding more tasks does not always improve performance. Geometry and occupancy trained together achieve 11.82% occupancy mIoU, compared with 11.53% for the three-task model that also includes detection (Tab. 16). Better task weighting and data sampling may help the model benefit more consistently from joint supervision, but testing new recipes is costly. For efficiency, our training schedule introduces Gaussian reconstruction after perception pretraining, deferring the cost of Gaussian decoding and rendering. Perception training took approximately 18 days, followed by another 9 days for Gaussian head training and joint fine-tuning. Although the final stage jointly optimizes the perception and Gaussian heads, we have not studied the benefits of training them together from the outset or systematically evaluated how geometry and rendering supervision affect each other. 42 Foundation4D: Towards unified perception and reconstruction model for autonomous vehicles Geometry. Depth errors increase at long range and around object boundaries (Figs. 6 and 7). Distant objects and thin structures occupy few pixels, making their depth difficult to estimate reliably. Differences in camera capture times can also affect pose estimation: rig supervision can mix fixed camera calibration with ego motion between exposures. Interpolating the ego trajectory does not resolve this ambiguity. Detection and tracking. Detection errors in crowded scenes and at long range also affect tracking. Missed objects and temporary confidence drops interrupt the observations available for association, leading to fragmented trajectories. Reliable long-video tracking therefore requires both more stable detections and better recovery across gaps in the observations. Semantic occupancy. Occupancy accuracy decreases at long range, and rare classes are often missed or assigned incorrect semantic labels. Predictions also fluctuate between frames, particularly around object boundaries and thin structures. Improving the coverage of rare classes in the training data and encouraging consistent predictions across frames may help reduce these errors. 10. Conclusion We presented Foundation4D, unified model for perception and reconstruction from multi-camera driving video. Shared visual features support geometry, objects, semantic occupancy, and Gaussian reconstruction, while video-level alignment and tracking extend its predictions to long driving sequences. To support learning and evaluation, our annotation pipeline addresses sensor timing, motion, and visibility when generating dense depth and semantic occupancy labels. The released PAIFoundation4D benchmark makes these annotations available for comparing geometry, detection, and occupancy methods on the same driving scenes. Our evaluations show both the value of temporal observations and the limits of the current joint-training recipe. Longer input windows improve detection without retraining, and trajectory refinement improves pose estimation across windows. In our task-combination study, detection performs best with all three tasks, while occupancy performs best when paired with geometry. The predicted geometry and trajectories also provide priors for lidarless NuRec, demonstrating their use in reconstruction for simulation. Improving the balance between tasks and understanding the interaction between geometric and rendering supervision remain open directions. 43 Foundation4D: Towards unified perception and reconstruction model for autonomous vehicles A.
